Thanks for the demo last week — the Optimize toolkit looks promising for our inference pipeline. Before we move to a pilot, the procurement and finance teams asked for a pricing structure that ties discounts to observable efficiency wins rather than a flat commit. Specifically we are thinking of a conditional rebate schedule based on: average per-request token cost (post-optimize), KV-cache hit rate, and the percent reduction from current model footprint gained via your recommended quantization profiles.

Two quick asks:
- Can you share an example of how Redwood would structure staged rebates linked to KV hit-rate thresholds and batching throughput?
- On quantization: what are your recommended profiles for customers who cannot tolerate >1% quality regression? Any guidance on expected latency impact for int8 vs int4?

I've attached a usage snapshot (OrionAI_usage_snapshot.csv) that shows our traffic patterns. We're open to a small reserved commitment for the pilot if you suggest it helps lock a rebate.

Appreciate a short write-up we can share with procurement.

Best,

Hi Maya — great to hear from you, and thanks for the usage dump.

Short answer: yes — we commonly structure conditional rebates that vest as customers hit operational efficiency milestones measured by our telemetry. High-level proposal (summary):

- Staged rebate schedule (pilot example):
  - Month 1 (pilot ramp): no rebate, baseline measurement window.
  - Month 2: 10% credit back for sustained KV-cache hit rate >= 45% and batching average >= 8 requests/slot.
  - Month 3+: additional 10% (total 20%) when KV-cache hit >= 60% and average latency SLO met (p95 <= 220ms).
  - Upside: further one-off rebate up to 5% for verified quantization gains that reduce GPU-hours by >= 15% without exceeding your 1% quality degradation threshold.

- Measurement & audit: Redwood will provide a telemetry package (per-route token cost, cache-hit rate, quant-impact delta) and a monthly verification report. Rebate credits apply to future invoice line items.

- Commit mechanics: you can choose a small reserved band for the pilot (e.g., 4 GPUs equivalent / monthly minimum) to get better baseline pricing; rebates are structured on top of that.

On quantization profiles (brief):
- Default recommended path: post-training static int8 -> evaluate quality on your validation prompts. Many customers hit <0.5% quality delta with int8.
- Conservative path: mixed-precision (fp16 for attention blocks, int8 for matmuls) for minimal risk.
- Aggressive path: int4 for embeddings/FFN with fallback to int8 for critical layers — this can yield the biggest cost wins but requires thorough functional evals.

I'll loop in Kimberly (quantization benchmarking) and Camila (commercial mechanics). Attached a short primer that explains how rebates are typically staged.

Next step: Kimberly will propose expected latency deltas and a rollback guardrail plan you can use in procurement language. If that looks good, we can draft a pilot order and a short SOW.

- Rishi

Subject: Re: Optimize toolkit pricing and conditional rebates — quantization and latency notes

Hi Maya — following up with technical guardrails and conservative performance expectations so procurement has language to act on.

Summary of recommendations (based on the usage profile you shared):
- Baseline: current model (fp16) on A100-like hardware — median latency 160ms, p95 310ms (approx from your snapshot).
- int8 (post-training static quant): expected median latency improvement ~8-12%, p95 typically improves ~5-10% assuming same batch sizing. Quality impact: most customers see <0.6% degradation on Nucleus metrics when we preserve attention scaling.
- int4 (aggressive): median latency improvement ~20-30%, p95 variable and depends on kernel availability — quality degradation risk increases; expect 0.8-2.5% on sensitive NLU tasks unless we do layer-wise selective fallbacks.

Operational guardrails we recommend embedding in the pilot SOW:
- Quantization rollback triggers: if eval-quality delta > 1% on a defined prompt set for 3 consecutive days, auto-fallback to int8.
- Canary window: enable quantization only for 5% of production traffic for 72 hours with active monitoring on hallucination/accuracy signals.
- KV-cache tuning: for your traffic shape, aim for a 50-65% cache hit target; that range delivers the bulk of token savings without increasing cold-start latency significantly.

I've attached lightweight benchmark artifacts we ran on similar traffic plus a quick chart of cache hit vs cost-savings.

Camila — for commercial language, I recommend the rebate table Rishi outlined but explicitly state the verification metrics and rollback rights for Orion procurement.

Happy to hop on a 30-min call to walk procurement through the technical bits.

Kimberly Park
Principal Applied ML — Inference Optimizations
